questions.q: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM customers returns 4,000 rows, the same as counting distinct customer_id values. What does this tell you?
options: The table has no duplicates
The duplicate rows are exact copies, so keeping one row per customer_id loses nothing
DISTINCT is broken in SQLite
Customer IDs are reused for different people
questions.explain: If rows with the same customer_id were different, SELECT DISTINCT * would keep more than 4,000. Getting 4,000 shows the extra 40 rows are identical copies.

questions.q: In the extract, why does ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY rowid) followed by rn = 1 remove duplicates?
options: It deletes rows from the customers table
It sorts the table permanently
It numbers rows within each customer_id, so keeping row 1 leaves one row per customer
It changes every customer_id to be unique
questions.explain: The window function numbers the rows inside each customer_id partition. Filtering to rn = 1 keeps one row per customer without modifying the underlying table.

questions.q: What happens when SQLite averages a text column that contains values like '$119.8'?
options: It raises an error
It skips those rows
It strips the dollar sign automatically
It reads them as 0, so the average is silently too low
questions.explain: SQLite converts text to a number by reading up to the first non-numeric character, so a leading dollar sign gives 0. Here 1,406 rows became zeros and the average dropped from 65.56 to 64.92.

questions.q: Why does every feature subquery in the extract include WHERE order_date <= :snap (or created_at <= :snap)?
options: To make the query run faster only
So features use only information available at the snapshot, preventing leakage from the future
Because SQLite requires a WHERE clause
To remove customers who churned
questions.explain: Orders dated after the snapshot exist in the data. Without the filter, the minimum days_ago would be -2, and recency and recent-order counts would use the future.

questions.q: The extract uses LEFT JOIN to attach order and ticket features. What does this ensure?
options: Customers with no orders or tickets stay in the population instead of disappearing
Every customer has at least one ticket
Duplicate rows are created for each order
Only churned customers are kept
questions.explain: An inner join would drop customers with no orders or tickets. LEFT JOIN keeps all 3,690 active customers, and COALESCE turns their missing counts into zeros.
